question: A city government proposes an AI system that would assign residents a general trustworthiness rating from unrelated public records, used by multiple departments to decide access to discretionary services. Under a risk-tiered AI regulatory framework, what is the most likely classification?
options: A. Minimal risk, because every one of the underlying records is already available to the public on request.
B. Limited risk, requiring only that residents are told a rating exists.
C. High risk, permitted once a conformity assessment has been completed.
D. A prohibited practice, because general social scoring by public authorities is banned.
rationale: Risk-tiered frameworks reserve an outright prohibition for a small set of practices, and general social scoring of individuals by public authorities across unrelated contexts is among them. Prohibited means unavailable at any level of documentation, which is why the high-risk answer is wrong: a conformity assessment cannot license a practice the framework forbids.

question: A European distributor buys an AI-enabled inspection system built by a manufacturer outside the region and resells it unchanged under the original brand. The distributor believes obligations rest entirely with the manufacturer. Is that correct?
options: A. No — importers and distributors carry duties of their own.
B. Yes — obligations attach only to the provider that developed and trained the system.
C. Yes — reselling without modification transfers all responsibility to the end deployer.
D. No — reselling a system unchanged makes the distributor the provider for all regulatory purposes.
rationale: AI-specific law differentiates obligations by organisational context: providers, deployers, importers and distributors each carry duties. An importer or distributor must satisfy itself that required documentation and conformity steps exist before placing a system on the market. It does not thereby become the provider, which is why the fourth option overstates the position as badly as the first two understate it.

question: A company is preparing a high-risk AI system for the EU market. Select the three obligations that must be satisfied before the system is placed on the market.
options: A. A conformity assessment appropriate to the system's classification.
B. Publication of the model's full training dataset for independent inspection.
C. Technical documentation sufficient to demonstrate the system meets its requirements.
D. A risk management process operating across the system's lifecycle.
E. Certification of the developing organisation against an information security standard.
rationale: Conformity assessment, technical documentation and lifecycle risk management are core pre-market requirements for high-risk systems, alongside data governance and record keeping. Publishing the training dataset is not required and would often be unlawful, and no AI framework conditions market access on the developer holding an information security certification.

question: A team is designing a model that flags university applications for manual review. Engineering proposes optimising for overall accuracy and setting the review threshold once the model is trained. What should governance require instead?
options: A. That overall accuracy be replaced entirely by a single fairness metric as the model's optimisation target.
B. That the threshold be set by whichever value produces the fewest manual reviews.
C. That success metrics and thresholds be defined during design, across applicant groups.
D. That the model be trained on the full applicant history before any metric is chosen.
rationale: Metric and threshold evaluation is a design-phase activity, not a post-training adjustment. Choosing them beforehand fixes what the system is trying to achieve and how failure will be recognised, including how error is distributed across groups. Replacing accuracy outright, minimising workload, or deferring until after training all let the metric be chosen to flatter the result.

question: A government agency is designing an AI system to prioritise applications for a hardship benefit. The design team is drawn entirely from engineering and finance. Which design-phase activity is most clearly missing?
options: A. A benchmark comparing the planned model against the commercially available alternatives on the market.
B. Stakeholder engagement with caseworkers and applicant representatives.
C. A pilot restricted to applications already approved through the manual process.
D. A decision on whether the model will run on agency infrastructure or in the cloud.
rationale: Stakeholder engagement and feedback is a named part of applying policies and best practice when designing a system. The people who administer the benefit and those who receive it hold information about failure modes that engineering and finance cannot supply. Benchmarking, pilot scope and hosting are real decisions that do not surface who the design might harm.

question: A payments company has finished testing a fraud model and the team wants to release. Governance asks what has to be true before production. Which answer best describes a release readiness gate?
options: A. That the model outperformed the incumbent on the held-out test set.
B. That the engineering team has the capacity to support the system through the months after launch.
C. That the release date has been communicated to affected internal teams.
D. That defined criteria — performance, documentation, conformity, rollback — are met and recorded.
rationale: Assessing readiness and preparing for release means testing the release against criteria agreed in advance and recording the result, so that a go decision is auditable and a no-go is possible. Beating the incumbent is one input among several, and support capacity and internal communication are launch logistics rather than a readiness standard.

question: A retailer's recommendation model is retrained nightly from live customer interactions. Security asks what periodic assessment should cover beyond ordinary performance monitoring.
options: A. Threat modelling and adversarial testing of the training pipeline.
B. Renegotiation of the cloud hosting agreement in order to secure improved availability terms overall.
C. Verification that recommendation latency remains within the agreed service target.
D. Confirmation that the model's accuracy has not fallen below its launch measurement.
rationale: Periodic activities to assess a system include audits, red teaming, threat modelling and security testing. A pipeline that learns continuously from user-influenced data is exposed to deliberate manipulation of its training inputs, which no accuracy or latency measure detects. Hosting terms are commercial, and latency and accuracy are the ordinary monitoring the question already excludes.

question: A logistics company's route optimisation model begins producing unusable routes for one region. Engineering identifies the immediate cause within a day. What does governance require beyond the fix?
options: A. Suspension of the model in all regions until the fix has run for a full quarter.
B. Reassignment of model ownership to the regional operations team most affected by the failure itself.
C. Documentation of the incident and cross-functional review of why it arose.
D. A public statement describing the failure and the corrective action taken.
rationale: Managing and documenting incidents, and collaborating with cross-functional stakeholders to understand why they arise — brittleness, data quality, insufficient testing, drift — is a named maintenance responsibility. The immediate cause explains the symptom; the review explains why controls did not catch it. Global suspension, reassignment and public disclosure are responses to different problems.

question: An energy utility retrains its demand model only when someone notices the forecasts have become unreliable. Over two years this has happened three times, each after weeks of degraded output. What should replace this practice?
options: A. A policy of retraining the model immediately after any forecast miss exceeds tolerance once.
B. Continuous monitoring with a defined maintenance, update and retraining schedule.
C. A switch to a simpler statistical model that is less sensitive to changing conditions.
D. An annual external audit of the model's forecasting performance and methodology.
rationale: Conducting continuous monitoring and establishing a regular schedule for maintenance, updates and retraining is the named control. Waiting for someone to notice guarantees weeks of degraded output every time. Retraining on a single miss overreacts to noise, replacing the model abandons capability to avoid a maintenance problem, and an annual audit would detect the drift long after it caused harm.

question: A law firm wants an AI assistant that summarises privileged client documents. Confidentiality obligations prevent client material leaving firm-controlled infrastructure. Which deployment consideration follows most directly?
options: A. The assistant should be limited to documents drawn from client matters that have already concluded.
B. The firm should require every lawyer to review each summary before it is relied upon.
C. The firm should select the largest available model to minimise summarisation errors.
D. Deployment options must be evaluated, favouring on-premise or private hosting.
rationale: Understanding the differences in deployment options — cloud, on-premise, edge — is part of evaluating a deployment decision, and a constraint that data must not leave controlled infrastructure resolves directly to where the model runs. Restricting to closed matters, mandating review and choosing a larger model are all reasonable practices that leave the confidentiality constraint unaddressed.

question: An insurer needs to predict claim severity from twelve structured fields with a decade of labelled history. A team proposes a large language model. What is the strongest governance objection?
options: A. A model type poorly matched to a structured task adds opacity and cost.
B. Language models cannot be applied to numerical data under any circumstances.
C. Insurance regulators prohibit generative models in all claims-related processes.
D. The decade of historical claims data would first have to be converted into natural language form.
rationale: Understanding the differences between model types — classic versus generative among them — is part of the deployment decision. A well-understood tabular problem with abundant labels is where classic approaches are strongest and most explainable; reaching for a generative model imports opacity, cost and evaluation difficulty for no gain. The alternatives state prohibitions and technical impossibilities that do not exist.

question: A company wants an internal assistant to answer questions from an engineering handbook that is revised most weeks. Accuracy against the current text matters more than writing style. Which approach best fits?
options: A. Fine-tune a base model on the handbook and repeat the fine-tune after each revision.
B. Deploy the base model unchanged and instruct staff to verify answers against the handbook.
C. Use retrieval against the current handbook at query time, leaving the base model unmodified.
D. Train a model from scratch on the handbook so that no external content can influence answers.
rationale: Deployment options include using a model as is, fine-tuning it, or applying retrieval, and the choice follows the requirement. Content that changes weekly and must be answered accurately points to retrieval, which reads the current text at query time. Repeated fine-tuning is expensive and always lags, unmodified deployment does not know the handbook, and training from scratch is disproportionate.

question: A distribution business is deciding whether to deploy a third-party AI system for warehouse staffing. Select the three factors most relevant to the deployment decision itself.
options: A. Whether the intended use case is clearly defined with measurable business objectives.
B. Whether the vendor's user interface matches the company's internal design conventions.
C. Whether data of sufficient quality and availability exists to support the intended use.
D. Whether the workforce is prepared to operate and question the system appropriately.
E. Whether the vendor's engineering team is larger than that of competing suppliers.
rationale: Understanding the context of the use case covers business objectives, performance requirements, data availability, ethical considerations and workforce readiness. Interface conventions are an aesthetic preference, and supplier headcount is not evidence about the system being bought.

question: A vendor supplies its own completed impact assessment for an AI scheduling system and asks the buyer to accept it as satisfying the buyer's assessment obligation. How should the buyer respond?
options: A. Accept it, since the vendor understands the system's internals better than the buyer can.
B. Review it and perform its own assessment of the system as deployed in its context.
C. Reject it and commission an independent third party to repeat the work from scratch.
D. Accept it on condition the vendor indemnifies the buyer against any assessment error.
rationale: Performing or reviewing an impact assessment on the selected system is the deployer's activity. A vendor assessment is useful evidence about the system in general, but it cannot cover the buyer's population, use case or controls, which is where the impact actually lands. Wholesale acceptance skips the part only the buyer can do; commissioning a third party to start over discards useful work; and an indemnity transfers cost, not the obligation.

question: The committee meets to address the 14-point regional drop in approval rates. What should it do FIRST?
options: A. Establish whether the model, applicant mix, or marketing change drives the shift.
B. Suspend the model in that metropolitan area until the disparity is resolved.
C. Notify regulators that a fair-lending disparity has been detected in the portfolio.
D. Retrain the model on more recent data so that current conditions are reflected.
rationale: Monitoring produced a signal, not a diagnosis. Three candidate causes are on the table and the pack does not distinguish them. Suspension, notification and retraining are all defensible responses to particular causes, and all of them are premature before the cause is known — each carries its own cost and one of them would be wrong under two of the three hypotheses.

question: Credit Products argues the model cannot discriminate because race, sex, age and postal code were removed before training. Which feature in the model most directly undermines that argument?
options: A. Debt-to-income ratio, which reflects the applicant's current obligations.
B. Length of credit history, which measures time rather than any personal characteristic.
C. Device type at the point of application, which can correlate with removed characteristics.
D. Employment tenure, which the bank verifies against payroll records.
rationale: Removing a protected attribute does not remove the information it carried, because other features can stand in for it. Device type is a consumer-behaviour signal with no causal relationship to repayment and a well-understood association with income and demographics — a textbook proxy. The other three have a defensible relationship to credit risk, which is what makes the proxy the outlier rather than the crowd.

question: Credit Products proposes expanding the model to small-business lending without a second validation. Who is most appropriately accountable for that decision?
options: A. Model Risk Management, since it owns validation and the model inventory.
B. The AI governance committee, since the expansion changes the model's approved use.
C. The Credit Products group, since it owns the business outcome and funds the work.
D. The Chief Risk Officer personally, since the committee reports to that role.
rationale: Extending a model to a new population is a change of scope, not a continuation of the approved one. The body that authorised the original use is the body that must authorise the change. Model Risk Management performs the validation but does not decide what the bank uses a model for; the business proposing the change cannot approve its own scope extension; and vesting the decision in the chair personally would replace a cross-functional control with an individual one.

question: Before any expansion to small-business lending is approved, which THREE conditions should the committee require?
options: A. Independent validation against the small-business applicant population.
B. A documented rationale for why features validated on consumers transfer to businesses.
C. Resolution of the open regional disparity on the existing use.
D. A commitment from Credit Products to a higher approval volume target.
E. Removal of the underwriter override so the two products behave consistently.
rationale: Validation was performed on a consumer population and says nothing about businesses, so it must be repeated. Feature transferability is the specific assumption Credit Products is making, and an assumption load-bearing enough to be argued should be written down and tested. And an unresolved disparity on the current use is unresolved evidence about the model itself — expanding on top of it multiplies whatever is wrong. A volume target is a business goal, not a control, and removing human override would weaken oversight rather than strengthen it.

question: Underwriters can override the score but follow it 94% of the time, and must write a justification only when they depart from it. Which governance concern does this arrangement most directly raise?
options: A. The override rate is too low to satisfy the bank's own model inventory requirements.
B. Recording justifications only for departures leaves no evidence agreement was considered.
C. Underwriters lack the technical training to interpret a machine learning score band.
D. The model should be fully automated, since human review changes so few outcomes.
rationale: Oversight is meaningful only if it is capable of dissent, and the paperwork here is asymmetric: departing costs the underwriter an explanation, agreeing costs nothing. That makes agreement the path of least resistance and leaves the bank unable to show, for the 94%, whether a human exercised judgement or deferred. The number itself is not the problem — a well-calibrated model should mostly be agreed with — the absence of evidence either way is.

question: A recruiter reports that applicants with employment gaps over four months are almost never surfaced. What should Calderon do FIRST?
options: A. Ask the vendor to remove employment-gap sensitivity from the model.
B. Quantify the pattern against its own applicant and hiring data.
C. Stop using the tool until the vendor supplies a revised bias audit.
D. Add a recruiter instruction to review applicants with gaps manually.
rationale: What exists so far is one recruiter's impression drawn from a handful of referral hires. Calderon holds the applicant and outcome data needed to turn that into a measured rate, and it can do so without the vendor's cooperation. Every other option commits resources, contractual leverage or a process change on the strength of an anecdote — and a manual-review instruction would paper over the pattern rather than establish whether it exists.

question: The tool was classified as a recruitment SaaS purchase and the AI governance function was not consulted before signature. Which governance failure does this most directly represent?
options: A. Procurement exceeded its delegated authority by signing without Legal's involvement.
B. The vendor policy triaged on purchase category rather than on what the system decides.
C. The contract omitted an SLA appropriate to a business-critical hiring system.
D. Calderon failed to obtain the training data it needed to validate the model.
rationale: The failure is upstream of anything in the contract. A policy that routes by spend category will keep missing AI systems, because what makes this one consequential is that it filters people out of a hiring process — not that it is bought as software. Legal was involved, so the first option misstates the facts; an SLA and training-data access are real gaps, but they are consequences of the tool never entering AI governance review, not the reason it did not.

question: Calderon cannot inspect the model and configures it through three undocumented sliders. Which artifact would most improve its ability to govern the tool?
options: A. A copy of the vendor's training dataset for independent analysis.
B. The model weights, so Calderon's data team can reproduce the ranking.
C. Documentation of what each configuration control changes and which signals it affects.
D. A certificate showing the vendor holds a recognised information security accreditation.
rationale: Calderon's live governance problem is that it is operating controls whose effects it cannot predict — it is accountable for a configuration it does not understand. Documenting what the sliders do is both the most directly useful thing and the most realistically obtainable. Training data and weights are commercially unlikely and would demand capability Calderon does not have; a security accreditation addresses a different risk entirely.

question: The Chief People Officer wants to extend the tool to driver hiring, where a licence check and a regulated safety record already apply. Which TWO considerations most directly bear on that decision?
options: A. Whether ranking that is opaque to Calderon can be reconciled with a regulated safety determination.
B. Whether the vendor's audit, which covers race and sex, speaks to the signals driver hiring depends on.
C. Whether extending the licence to a second job family increases the per-applicant cost.
D. Whether recruiters prefer the tool's interface to the current driver hiring workflow.
E. Whether the Netherlands site would adopt the driver configuration at the same time.
rationale: Driver hiring sits on top of a regulated safety record, so an opaque ranking layer interacts with an obligation Calderon must be able to evidence. And the vendor's audit was scoped to race and sex on a warehouse population; nothing in it speaks to the signals a driving role turns on, so it cannot be carried across. Cost and interface preference are real considerations but not governance ones, and the Netherlands site is a separate question about jurisdiction rather than about extending the job family.

question: Calderon's Netherlands site uses the same tool for warehouse hiring. Which consideration most directly governs how that use must be treated?
options: A. Employment AI attracts heightened obligations, and Calderon is the deployer, not the provider.
B. The obligations fall entirely on the vendor, since it developed and trained the model.
C. The site is too small to bring the deployment within scope of any AI-specific regime.
D. Because the model was trained outside the EU, only the vendor's home jurisdiction applies.
rationale: AI used to filter candidates in recruitment is treated as a heightened-risk use under the EU regime, and the roles are distinct: the vendor that develops and places the system on the market is the provider, while the organisation using it under its own authority is the deployer. Deployer duties — human oversight, monitoring, use in line with the instructions — sit with Calderon and cannot be delegated back to the vendor by contract. Headcount does not determine scope, and neither does where training happened.

question: Review found 6% of drafted answers cited unsupportive passages and 2% cited superseded policy, all caught by caseworkers. Which finding should receive the highest priority?
options: A. The 6%, because unsupported citations are the larger share of the defects found.
B. The 2%, because a stale index yields confident answers that survive the check.
C. Neither, because the caseworker review step caught every case in the sample.
D. The 6%, because it indicates the underlying model is unsuitable for retrieval tasks.
rationale: The two defects fail differently against the control that catches them. An unsupported citation is visible to a caseworker doing the required check: the passage does not say what the answer claims. A superseded passage is not — the citation genuinely supports the answer, and the answer is genuinely wrong, so the check passes and the error survives. The smaller number is the more dangerous one because it defeats the control rather than being caught by it, and 'all caught in a 400-item sample' is a statement about this sample, not a guarantee.

question: Legal has raised, but not resolved, whether a drafted answer a caseworker relied on forms part of the determination record. What should happen BEFORE full deployment?
options: A. Extend log retention to six years for every query as a precaution.
B. Resolve the question, then set retention to match the answer.
C. Keep the 30-day schedule, since the assistant plays no part in eligibility decisions.
D. Stop logging drafted answers, so no new record category is created.
E. Ask the model provider what retention period it applies to API requests.
rationale: Retention is downstream of a records classification question that is still open, and either guess creates its own exposure: over-retaining spreads personal data across a six-year window with no basis, while under-retaining risks destroying records the department is required to keep. Deciding the classification is cheap and is the department's own call. Deleting logs to avoid creating records inverts the obligation, and the provider's retention says nothing about the department's schedule.

question: The department is assessing how tightly this deployment should be governed. Which fact most reduces the risk classification the assistant warrants?
options: A. Caseworkers, not residents, are the only users of the assistant.
B. The assistant produces no output that determines or informs eligibility.
C. The retrieval index is built from the department's own policy manuals.
D. Every query and drafted answer was logged during the pilot.
rationale: Risk classification follows what the system decides or influences, not who touches it. An AI system that plays no part in determining access to a public benefit sits outside the categories that attract heightened obligations, and that is the fact doing the work here. Restricting the audience to staff, sourcing the index internally and logging thoroughly are all sound controls, but a system that shaped eligibility would still be heightened-risk with every one of them in place.

question: The council has asked for a public statement about the department's use of AI. Which THREE elements most belong in it?
options: A. What the assistant is used for and what it is not used for.
B. That a caseworker reviews and is accountable for every answer given to a resident.
C. How a resident can raise a concern about the department's use of the assistant.
D. The name and version of the commercial model behind the assistant.
E. The measured error rates observed during the pilot review.
rationale: A meaningful public statement tells people what the system does, who remains answerable for the outcome, and how to challenge it — scope, accountability, redress. The model's name and version tell a resident nothing they can act on and will be stale within a release cycle. Pilot error rates are important governance evidence and belong in the department's internal record, but published without the context of the control that caught them they inform nobody and mislead many.

question: The provider guarantees only 90 days' deprecation notice and no version stability. Which monitoring control most directly addresses that dependency?
options: A. Negotiate a contractual guarantee that the model version will not change.
B. Run a fixed evaluation set on a schedule and after any provider change.
C. Increase the sample size of the caseworker answer review from 400 to 1,000 items.
D. Mirror the provider's model locally so the department controls the version in use.
rationale: The department cannot control when the model changes, so the control has to be detection: a stable evaluation set turns an invisible upstream change into a visible movement in a number the department owns. A version guarantee is not on offer from a general-purpose provider and would not survive the next deprecation cycle. A larger review sample measures the same thing more precisely without telling anyone when it moved, and self-hosting a commercial model is not available and would transfer obligations the department is not resourced to hold.

question: A university is building a model to flag undergraduates at risk of dropping out so advisers can reach them early. The training set is ten years of student records. Which characteristic of that data most warrants examination before training begins?
options: A. Whether the records are stored in a system that supports row-level access control.
B. Whether past adviser interventions influenced the outcomes the model will learn to predict.
C. Whether the records span enough years to give the model sufficient volume.
D. Whether the file format the registry exports is convenient for the modelling toolchain.
rationale: The outcome being predicted was not observed in a vacuum: advisers already intervened with some students, and those interventions changed who dropped out. A model trained on that history learns the world as it was after the intervention, and will systematically misjudge what happens without one. Storage controls, volume and file format are real project concerns that do not touch the validity of the label.

question: An insurer is preparing to validate a claims-triage model. Which practice most strengthens the independence of that validation?
options: A. Running validation on the same held-out split that the development team already used.
B. Having validation performed by staff outside the development owner's reporting line.
C. Requiring the development team to document its own testing in more detail.
D. Scheduling validation to conclude before the product launch date is announced.
rationale: Independence is a reporting-line property, not a documentation or scheduling one. A reviewer whose appraisal is written by the person whose model they are reviewing is not positioned to fail it. Reusing the development team's split imports whatever selection decisions were made there; better documentation improves the record without changing who judges it; and a timetable says nothing about who holds the pen.

question: A telecommunications provider's churn model performed well in testing and poorly in its first month live. Investigation shows a feature used in training is computed from data that is only complete 40 days after a customer interaction. What does this most likely indicate?
options: A. The model was overfitted to the training data and needs stronger regularisation.
B. The feature carried information unavailable at prediction time, inflating test performance.
C. The production infrastructure is too slow to serve the model within its latency budget.
D. The customer population changed materially between training and deployment.
rationale: A feature that takes 40 days to settle is complete in a historical dataset and incomplete when a live prediction is made. The model was scored in testing with knowledge it can never have in production, which is why the two numbers disagree. Overfitting, latency and population shift all produce degradation too, but none of them explains a gap that appears specifically between a retrospective dataset and a real-time one.

question: A consumer electronics manufacturer is documenting a defect-detection model before release. Which content makes the documentation most useful to whoever operates the model in two years?
options: A. A record of the architectures the team evaluated and discarded during development.
B. The conditions the model was tested under, and where it should not be relied on.
C. A summary of the compute budget and training duration for the final run.
D. Biographies of the data scientists who built and validated the system.
rationale: Documentation earns its keep when someone who was not there has to decide whether the model still applies. Stated operating conditions and stated limits are what let a future operator recognise that the line, the lighting or the product has drifted outside what was tested. Discarded architectures, compute spend and team biographies are project history — they explain how the model came to exist, not when to stop trusting it.

question: A grid operator plans to use synthetic data to augment a scarce set of equipment-failure examples. Which risk most specifically attaches to that choice?
options: A. Synthetic records may reproduce the generator's assumptions rather than real failures.
B. Synthetic data increases the storage footprint of the training pipeline.
C. Synthetic data cannot be used in models that will operate on physical infrastructure.
D. Synthetic records must be individually approved by the data protection officer.
rationale: Synthetic data can only express what its generator was built to express. If the generator learned from the same scarce failures, the augmented set inherits their blind spots and reports back a confidence the evidence does not support — the model looks better tested than it is. Storage is trivial, no rule bars synthetic data from physical systems, and approval requirements attach to personal data rather than to equipment telemetry.

question: A retailer's demand-forecasting team wants to move a model from pilot to production. Which evidence best supports a release decision?
options: A. Pilot evaluation performance, broken down by product category and store format.
B. Confirmation that the pilot ran without unplanned outages for its full duration.
C. Endorsement from the category managers who took part in the pilot.
D. A comparison showing the model outperforms the previous forecast on aggregate error.
rationale: An aggregate number hides exactly the failure a retailer cares about: a model can beat the incumbent overall while being worse in a category or store format that matters. Disaggregated performance is what shows where the model can be relied on and where it cannot. Uptime is an operational fact, user endorsement is a satisfaction signal, and a single aggregate comparison is the average that disaggregation exists to interrogate.

question: A software company is red-teaming a customer-facing generative feature before launch. Which finding should most delay the release?
options: A. Testers produced offensive output using prompts no ordinary customer would write.
B. Ordinary product questions caused the feature to reveal another customer's data.
C. Testers found the feature's tone inconsistent across a long conversation.
D. Response latency exceeded the target on a small share of long prompts.
rationale: Severity and reachability have to be read together. A cross-customer data disclosure reached through ordinary use is both serious and certain to recur, because nothing stands between a normal user and it. Offensive output from contrived prompts is real but bounded by the effort needed to trigger it; inconsistent tone and occasional latency are quality issues that do not put anyone's data in someone else's hands.

question: A bank's model inventory lists 340 models. Governance capacity allows deep review of about 40 a year. Which basis for selecting them best serves the inventory's purpose?
options: A. The models that consume the largest share of the organisation's compute budget.
B. The models whose failure would most affect customers or regulatory obligations.
C. The models that have gone longest without a documentation refresh.
D. The models that the largest number of internal teams depend on.
rationale: An inventory exists so that finite assurance effort lands where failure costs most. Consequence — to customers and to obligations the bank must be able to evidence — is the ordering that serves that purpose. Compute spend measures cost rather than risk; time since last refresh is a useful trigger but treats a trivial model and a critical one alike; and internal dependency counts reach rather than harm.

question: During development of a hiring-adjacent model, the team finds a feature that improves accuracy but has no explainable relationship to job performance. What is the most appropriate response?
options: A. Retain it, because accuracy on the validation set is the agreed selection criterion.
B. Investigate what the feature is standing in for before deciding whether to retain it.
C. Remove it immediately, since unexplainable features cannot be used in employment contexts.
D. Retain it but exclude it from the model documentation to avoid confusing reviewers.
rationale: An unexplained predictive feature is a question, not yet a verdict. It may encode something legitimate the team has not articulated, or it may be a proxy for a protected characteristic — and those two lead to opposite decisions, so the investigation has to come first. Keeping it on accuracy alone accepts an unexamined risk; discarding it reflexively throws away signal on a rule that does not exist; and omitting it from documentation would conceal the very thing a reviewer needs to see.

question: A logistics company fine-tunes an open-weight model on its internal operations manuals. Which governance obligation does fine-tuning most clearly introduce?
options: A. Establishing that the licence for the base model permits the intended use.
B. Publishing the fine-tuned weights so downstream users can inspect them.
C. Registering the fine-tuned model with the base model's original developer.
D. Retraining the model from scratch to avoid inheriting base-model behaviour.
rationale: Open weights are not the same as unrestricted use: base models ship under licences that vary in what they permit commercially, in what they require downstream, and in what use they prohibit. Checking that the intended use is inside those terms is the obligation that attaches at the moment of fine-tuning. Publication, registration and full retraining are not general requirements, and the last would discard the reason for fine-tuning at all.

question: A pharmaceutical company's research team wants to use a third-party dataset whose provenance the supplier will not fully describe. Which TWO risks should most influence the decision?
options: A. That the data may not be lawfully available for the intended purpose.
B. That undisclosed collection methods may bias the population the data represents.
C. That the dataset may require more storage than the current environment provides.
D. That the supplier may raise its price at the next contract renewal.
E. That the file schema may need transformation before it can be loaded.
rationale: Undisclosed provenance leaves two things unknowable, and both are load-bearing. Legally, the company cannot establish that it may use the data for this purpose, and unlawful inputs contaminate everything built on them. Scientifically, how the data was collected determines who is in it — and a population shaped by an undisclosed method will produce findings that do not generalise. Storage, price and schema are procurement and engineering matters that do not turn on provenance at all.

question: A streaming service discovers its recommendation model amplifies a narrow set of titles, reducing catalogue diversity. Engineering proposes a fix; the product team objects that engagement metrics will fall. Which consideration should govern the decision?
options: A. Whether the engagement decline would be recovered within the next quarter.
B. Whether concentration is a harm the organisation has committed to managing.
C. Whether competitors' recommenders show comparable concentration.
D. Whether the engineering fix can be delivered without a full model retrain.
rationale: This is a values conflict between two legitimate objectives, and it is settled by what the organisation has already committed to — a stated principle, a published policy, an internal standard. If concentration is a named harm, the trade-off has been decided in advance and this is an implementation question; if it is not, the organisation is making the commitment now and should do so explicitly. Recovery timelines, competitor behaviour and implementation cost inform how to act, not whether the harm counts.

question: The vendor claims flag rates are comparable across demographic groups but will not supply the analysis. How should Northbridge treat that claim?
options: A. As satisfied, since the vendor is contractually responsible for its own product claims.
B. As unverified, and obtain evidence proportionate to what the university is accountable for.
C. As irrelevant, since an integrity officer reviews every flag before a case opens.
D. As disqualifying, since any withheld analysis makes a vendor unusable.
rationale: A claim the deployer cannot examine is not evidence, and Northbridge remains accountable for outcomes on its own students whatever the contract says. That does not make the vendor unusable — proportionate alternatives exist, including a summary under confidentiality, an independent attestation, or the university's own monitoring of flag rates once live.

question: Disability services notes that some conditions produce atypical gaze patterns. Which action best addresses the risk this creates?
options: A. Disable gaze detection for every candidate so that no group is disadvantaged by it.
B. Ask flagged students to disclose any relevant condition during the review.
C. Build the existing accommodations process into the flag review before a case can open.
D. Record the interaction in the risk register and monitor case outcomes for a term.
rationale: The university already runs an accommodations process; the failure would be a review pipeline that does not consult it, so a flagged student with a known accommodation is assessed as though they had none. Connecting the two is targeted and uses machinery that exists. Disabling the signal for everyone discards a control the tool was licensed for, asking students to disclose at the point of accusation puts the burden in the wrong place, and monitoring alone observes harm rather than preventing it.

question: The model is retrained weekly on data that includes its own prior pricing decisions. What risk does this most directly create?
options: A. The training set grows faster than the pricing team can review it.
B. The model treats its own past choices as evidence about demand, reinforcing them.
C. The model becomes more sensitive to competitor prices over successive retrainings.
D. Weekly retraining is too frequent for the model to reach stable performance.
rationale: The transactions the model learns from are the transactions its own prices produced. If it priced a segment high and saw fewer sales, it learns that the segment has lower demand — when what it observed was its own decision. Left unexamined, the loop entrenches early choices and drifts away from real demand. Data volume, competitor sensitivity and retraining frequency are all plausible-sounding, and none of them describes the feedback loop.

question: Legal notes that approximate location correlates with income in several markets. The pricing team responds that no protected attribute was given to the model. Which consideration should carry the most weight?
options: A. Whether the correlation produces materially different outcomes for protected groups.
B. Whether the pricing team documented the exclusion of protected attributes before training.
C. Whether competitors in the same markets use comparable location signals.
D. Whether customers can determine their displayed price is location-dependent.
rationale: Intent is not the test; effect is. A model given no protected attribute can still allocate systematically different prices along one, and what matters is whether the outcome difference is material and whether Vantor owes anyone a duty about it. Documenting the exclusion evidences good process without answering the question, competitor practice is a benchmark rather than a standard, and customer awareness is a transparency matter that leaves the distribution unchanged.

question: Vantor's public policy says prices 'vary with demand and availability'. Which TWO issues does that disclosure most directly raise?
options: A. It omits that an automated system sets prices using session-level signals.
B. It may not meet the standard of clarity expected in Vantor's stricter markets.
C. It fails to publish the model's feature weightings for customer inspection.
D. It does not name the vendor that supplied the pricing technology.
E. It does not commit Vantor to a maximum price change in any 24-hour period.
rationale: The gap is between what the disclosure says and what the system does: 'demand and availability' would describe a stock-based rule, not an automated model reading location and device. That omission also has to be read against the markets Vantor sells into, which set different bars for how plainly automated processing must be explained. Feature weights, vendor identity and a volatility cap are not standard disclosure obligations, and publishing weights would tell a customer nothing they could use.

question: Ardal must show that maintenance decisions affecting supply reliability are traceable to an accountable person. Under the pilot, work orders carry the agent's identifier. What is the most appropriate response?
options: A. Record the engineering lead as accountable for all orders the agent issues.
B. Define who is accountable for the agent's dispatch decisions and record that on each order.
C. Treat the agent's identifier as sufficient, since it traces the decision to its source.
D. Return to planner-issued orders, since automated dispatch cannot satisfy the requirement.
rationale: Accountability attaches to a person, and automating an action does not move the duty — it moves who must be named. The task is to decide whose authority the agent acts under and to make that visible on the artifact the regulator inspects. Naming the engineering lead by default assigns accountability by convenience rather than by authority; a system identifier traces provenance but is not a person; and abandoning automation treats an evidencing problem as though it were a prohibition.

question: The engineering lead cites 61 cancellations out of 4,100 as evidence the agent performs well. What is the strongest objection to that reasoning?
options: A. Eight weeks is too short a pilot to draw conclusions about a dispatch system.
B. Cancellations count errors planners happened to catch, not errors that occurred.
C. The comparison should be against the ranking model's 18% override rate.
D. A 1.5% cancellation rate is high for a system issuing safety-relevant work orders.
rationale: Nobody reviews orders before issue, so a cancellation records the subset of bad dispatches a planner noticed in time. The rate measures the detection process at least as much as the agent, and the denominator for undetected errors is unknown. Pilot length is a fair general caution but weaker than a flaw in the metric itself; the 18% override rate belongs to a different system doing a different job; and calling 1.5% high asserts a threshold the facts do not supply.

question: The operations director identifies a known worst case that has not yet occurred: dispatching a crew to a transformer another crew has de-energised. How should this be treated relative to the 44 duplicate dispatches already observed?
options: A. As lower priority, since it has not occurred during the pilot.
B. As the same issue at higher severity, arising from the same 15-minute staleness.
C. As a separate risk requiring a control unrelated to the duplicate dispatches.
D. As acceptable, since a planner can cancel any order before a crew arrives.
rationale: Both failures come from one cause: the agent acts on availability data up to fifteen minutes old. The duplicates are the low-severity expression of it and the de-energised transformer is the high-severity one, so a control that fixes the staleness addresses both. Treating the severe case as lower priority because it has not happened yet mistakes absence of occurrence for absence of exposure, and planner cancellation is exactly the control that let 44 duplicates through.

question: Ardal wants to keep the dispatch agent but reduce its exposure. Which TWO changes address the underlying cause rather than its symptoms?
options: A. Read crew availability from the real-time crew management system rather than the 15-minute feed.
B. Hold any dispatch to a site with recent crew activity until availability is confirmed current.
C. Raise the confidence threshold the ranking model must exceed before an order is issued.
D. Require a planner to review every dispatched order within one hour of issue.
E. Increase the cancellation window so planners have longer to intervene.
rationale: The cause is a decision taken on stale state. Reading the authoritative real-time source removes the staleness, and gating dispatches to recently active sites contains the residual case where currency cannot be confirmed. Raising the ranking threshold changes which transformers are prioritised, which is a different system and a different problem; post-issue review and a longer cancellation window both widen the net for catching a bad order rather than preventing it.

question: A software vendor sells an AI-enabled product across the EU. It substantially modifies the system's intended purpose and re-releases it under its own brand. What is the most direct governance consequence?
options: A. The original developer retains all provider obligations for the modified system.
B. The vendor takes on provider obligations for the system as modified.
C. Obligations are shared proportionally between the two organisations.
D. Neither party holds obligations until the modified system is first sold.
rationale: Provider status follows who puts a system on the market under their own name and who determines its intended purpose. Substantially modifying the purpose and re-releasing under your own brand is precisely what transfers that role. Obligations do not stay with the original developer for a system it no longer defines, are not apportioned by negotiation, and attach on placing on the market rather than at first sale.

question: An organisation already runs a mature information security management system and wants to add AI governance. Which statement best describes the relationship between the two?
options: A. The AI management system replaces the security management system for AI assets.
B. AI governance can reuse the existing management-system structure, adding AI controls.
C. The two must be maintained as entirely separate systems with separate audits.
D. Security certification satisfies AI governance requirements for systems already in scope.
E. AI governance applies only to systems that process personal data.
rationale: Management-system standards share a common structure — context, leadership, planning, support, operation, evaluation, improvement — which is what lets an organisation run them together rather than in parallel. The AI-specific part is what gets added: impact assessment, lifecycle controls, data governance for AI. Replacement, forced separation, and treating security certification as covering AI all misread that relationship, and AI governance is not scoped to personal data.

question: A risk management framework organises AI risk work into governing, mapping, measuring and managing. Which activity belongs to mapping rather than measuring?
options: A. Selecting metrics for a system's performance across subgroups.
B. Establishing the context, intended use and affected parties of a system.
C. Running an evaluation against a held-out dataset before a release decision is taken.
D. Deciding which identified risks to accept, transfer or mitigate.
rationale: Mapping establishes what the system is for, where it operates and who it affects — the context that makes any later measurement meaningful. Choosing metrics and running evaluations are measurement activities, and deciding what to do with an identified risk is management. The distinction matters because measuring before mapping produces precise numbers about the wrong thing.

question: A company deploys the same AI-enabled hiring tool in a jurisdiction with a specific automated-employment-decision law and in one without. Which approach best manages the difference?
options: A. Apply the stricter jurisdiction's controls everywhere unless there is a reason not to.
B. Apply each jurisdiction's minimum requirement, so nothing exceeds what is required.
C. Apply the looser standard everywhere and document the gap as an accepted risk.
D. Suspend use in the stricter jurisdiction until a local variant of the tool is available.
rationale: A single high baseline is cheaper to operate and to evidence than several divergent ones, and it avoids the failure mode where a system quietly crosses a border. It is a default, not a dogma — where a stricter control conflicts with local law or is genuinely disproportionate, the exception should be reasoned and recorded. Per-jurisdiction minima multiply configurations and audit surface, the looser standard everywhere accepts a known breach, and suspension forgoes the tool where it is most scrutinised.

question: Under GDPR, an organisation relies on legitimate interests to process personal data for training a fraud-detection model. What does that basis most directly require it to do?
options: A. Obtain explicit consent from each data subject before training begins.
B. Balance its interest against data subjects' rights and expectations, and record it.
C. Anonymise the training data so that the lawful basis no longer applies.
D. Register the processing activity with the supervisory authority before it starts.
rationale: Legitimate interests is the basis that carries a balancing test: the controller must identify the interest, show the processing is necessary for it, and weigh it against the individuals' rights and reasonable expectations — documented, so it can be produced. Consent is a different basis, not a supplement to this one; anonymisation would take the data outside the regime entirely rather than satisfy the basis; and general prior registration is not a GDPR requirement.

question: An AI system is used by a bank to determine eligibility for essential services and by a games studio to balance difficulty. Both use similar underlying technology. What most explains why their governance obligations differ?
options: A. The bank operates in a regulated sector and the studio does not.
B. Obligations follow the consequences of the use, not the technology used.
C. The bank's system processes more personal data than the studio's.
D. The studio's system is unlikely to be reviewed by a supervisory authority.
rationale: Risk-based regulation attaches to what a system does to people, which is why identical technology can carry very different duties. Sector regulation is a consequence of the same reasoning rather than the explanation for it; data volume does not determine obligation; and likelihood of scrutiny describes enforcement, not what the law requires.

question: A model produces an output that its developers cannot fully explain in causal terms, but whose inputs, version and decision path are fully logged. Which property does the organisation have?
options: A. Interpretability, since the model's internal logic can be followed.
B. Traceability, since the decision can be reconstructed even if not explained.
C. Contestability, since a subject can challenge the outcome on the record.
D. Robustness, since the decision path is stable across runs.
rationale: Knowing exactly what went in, which version ran, and what came out is traceability — the ability to reconstruct a decision after the fact. It is not interpretability, which is being able to follow why the model behaved as it did. Traceability supports contestability without being it, and says nothing about robustness. Keeping the three apart matters because organisations often claim explainability when what they have built is a good audit log.

question: A company states a principle that its AI systems will be 'fair'. Which step most improves that principle's usefulness?
options: A. Publishing the principle prominently on the corporate website and in the annual report.
B. Defining what fairness means for each use case and how it will be measured.
C. Requiring every employee to complete training on the principle.
D. Appointing a senior executive as the owner of the principle.
rationale: Fairness has several incompatible formalisations, and a system can satisfy one while failing another — so an undefined commitment cannot be complied with, tested, or breached. Making it operational means saying which notion applies to which use and what evidence would show it. Publication, training and executive ownership all help a defined principle travel, and none of them supplies the definition.

question: Which TWO conditions most distinguish a governance committee that functions from one that exists on paper?
options: A. It can stop or condition a deployment, and that authority has been used.
B. Its membership spans the functions that would surface different risks.
C. It meets on a fixed calendar with minutes circulated to the executive.
D. It is chaired by the most senior available executive.
E. Its terms of reference are approved by the board.
rationale: Two things make a committee real: it can actually say no, and it contains the perspectives that would notice a problem in the first place. A body that has never exercised its authority may simply have had nothing to stop, but combined with narrow membership it usually means the authority is nominal. Meeting cadence, chair seniority and board-approved terms are hygiene — necessary scaffolding that a paper committee also has.

question: An organisation is deciding where its AI governance function should sit. Which consideration should weigh most heavily?
options: A. Whether the function can raise concerns without depending on the teams it reviews.
B. Whether the function reports to the executive with the largest technology budget.
C. Whether the function is co-located with the data science teams it works alongside.
D. Whether the function's headcount is comparable to peer organisations.
rationale: Placement decides whether an escalation can survive being unwelcome. A function whose budget, appraisal or standing depends on the teams it reviews will find its concerns getting softer over time, whatever its mandate says. Budget size, physical proximity and benchmark headcount describe resourcing and convenience, not whether the function can carry bad news upward.

question: A team describes its system as 'agentic'. Which characteristic most changes the governance approach compared with a predictive model?
options: A. It is built on a substantially larger model with more parameters and broader training.
B. It takes actions in other systems rather than only returning outputs.
C. It generates natural language rather than numeric scores.
D. It is accessed through an API rather than an internal library.
rationale: A predictive model produces something a human then acts on; an agent acts. That collapses the gap where review used to happen and makes the blast radius a function of what the agent can reach, so authorisation, scoping and reversibility become primary controls. Model size, output modality and integration method change engineering and cost without changing who or what the system can affect directly.

question: A team must choose an evaluation approach for a model whose errors are rare but costly. Which approach best fits?
options: A. Report overall accuracy, since it summarises performance in a single comparable number.
B. Evaluate on the error cases specifically, and report their performance separately.
C. Increase the test set size until the overall accuracy estimate stabilises.
D. Compare against a baseline model trained on the same data.
rationale: When the costly outcome is rare, overall accuracy is dominated by the common case and can stay excellent while the model fails at exactly the thing that matters. Evaluating and reporting the rare class separately puts the number that carries the risk in front of the decision-maker. A bigger test set makes the misleading average more precise, and a baseline comparison inherits whatever blind spot the metric has.

question: A financial services firm wants a single artifact that lets a reviewer two years from now assess whether a model is still fit for use. Which is most appropriate?
options: A. The training notebook, with cell outputs and intermediate results preserved.
B. Documentation of intended use, tested conditions, known limitations and monitoring assumptions.
C. A performance dashboard showing current metrics against thresholds.
D. The change log of every code commit made during development.
rationale: Fitness for use is a question about the gap between what a model was built and tested for and the world it now runs in — so the artifact has to state the original scope and its limits. A dashboard shows the present without the standard to judge it against; a notebook and a commit log record how the model was produced, which is provenance rather than applicability.

question: During validation, a reviewer finds the development team defined the target variable differently from the way the business uses the term. What is the most appropriate finding to raise?
options: A. A documentation defect, since the definition was never clearly written down anywhere.
B. A construct validity defect, since the model may not measure what the business intends.
C. A data quality defect, since the underlying records are inconsistently labelled.
D. A stakeholder engagement defect, since the business was not consulted enough.
rationale: If the modelled quantity is not the quantity the business means, then every downstream number is precise about the wrong thing, and no amount of accuracy repairs it. That is a validity problem with the construct itself. Poor documentation and thin consultation are very likely how it happened, and inconsistent labels are a different fault — none of them names what is actually broken.

question: A team proposes to measure a hiring model's fairness using a single statistical parity test across one protected attribute. Which limitation matters most?
options: A. Statistical parity is computationally expensive on large applicant populations.
B. One test on one attribute can pass while other attributes or intersections diverge.
C. Statistical parity requires access to protected attributes the firm may not hold.
D. Statistical parity is only meaningful when the model is fully automated.
rationale: A single metric on a single attribute is a narrow window. Groups defined by another attribute, or by the intersection of two, can be disadvantaged while the headline test passes — and intersectional disparities routinely hide behind marginal parity. Cost is negligible, attribute availability is a real practical obstacle rather than a limitation of the measure, and parity applies whether or not a human is in the loop.

question: Which THREE elements make a pre-deployment impact assessment useful rather than ceremonial?
options: A. It identifies who could be adversely affected and how.
B. It records decisions that were taken because of what it found.
C. It is completed early enough that its findings can still change the design.
D. It is signed by an executive sponsor before deployment proceeds.
E. It follows a template consistent with peer organisations in the sector.
rationale: An assessment earns its place by naming who bears the risk, arriving while the design can still move, and leaving a trace of what actually changed as a result. Those three are what separate an analysis from a form. A sponsor signature and a peer-consistent template make it auditable and comparable, and a ceremonial assessment has both.

question: A model's performance on a protected subgroup is materially worse, and the team finds the subgroup is under-represented in the training data. Which response addresses the cause?
options: A. Apply a post-processing adjustment so subgroup outcome rates match.
B. Obtain or construct better representation for the subgroup and re-evaluate.
C. Publish the subgroup performance gap alongside the model documentation.
D. Restrict the model's use to subgroups where performance meets the threshold.
rationale: The diagnosis in the facts is representation, so the treatment is representation. Post-processing can equalise a reported rate while leaving the model just as poorly informed about the subgroup; disclosure is honest but changes nothing; and restricting use excludes the group the system underserves, which converts a performance problem into an access one. All three are legitimate steps alongside the fix, and none of them is the fix.

question: An organisation's incident process was written for security incidents. Which addition is most necessary before it can handle AI incidents?
options: A. A faster notification timeline, since AI incidents propagate more quickly.
B. Criteria for recognising an incident where nothing failed technically.
C. A dedicated on-call rota staffed by the data science team.
D. Integration with the vendor's support ticketing system.
rationale: Security incident processes trigger on something breaking — an outage, an intrusion, a data loss. The characteristic AI incident is a system working exactly as built and producing a harmful or unfair outcome, which no availability or integrity alarm will raise. Without criteria for that, the process never starts. Timelines, rotas and ticketing integration all matter after something has been recognised as an incident.

question: A deployed model's inputs have shifted materially, but its accuracy on recent labelled data is unchanged. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: A. The shift is benign and requires no action beyond continued monitoring.
B. Input drift without performance loss still warrants investigating why it occurred.
C. The accuracy measurement is unreliable and should be recalculated.
D. The model should be retrained immediately to match the new input distribution.
rationale: Stable accuracy today is genuine reassurance, and it is not a cause. A shifted input distribution means something changed upstream — a new customer segment, a changed data pipeline, an altered collection method — and until you know which, you cannot say whether performance will hold. Declaring it benign skips the question, doubting the metric contradicts the evidence, and retraining on an unexplained shift risks fitting to a pipeline defect.

question: A support team begins using an internal generative tool to draft customer responses. No policy covered it, and no one approved it. Which risk should be addressed FIRST?
options: A. That the tool's licence terms may not permit commercial use of its generated output.
B. That customer data may already be leaving the organisation through the tool.
C. That drafted responses may be inconsistent with the brand's tone.
D. That the team may become dependent on a tool with no support contract.
rationale: Ordering by reversibility puts data egress first: it is happening now, if it is happening, and it cannot be undone once information has left. Licensing exposure accrues but is remediable, tone inconsistency is a quality matter, and dependency is a future problem. The habit worth building is to ask which risk is already realising and which cannot be walked back.

question: Which TWO conditions most justify treating a human-in-the-loop control as an effective mitigation?
options: A. The reviewer has the information and authority needed to reach a different conclusion.
B. The review happens before the consequential action, not after it.
C. The reviewer is a subject-matter expert in the model's technical architecture.
D. The review is recorded in an audit log retained for a defined period.
E. The reviewer handles a volume comparable to the pre-automation workload.
rationale: A human control mitigates only if the human can actually reach a different answer and does so while the outcome is still open. Missing either turns oversight into commentary. Understanding the architecture is rarely necessary — the reviewer needs the case, not the model internals — and an audit log evidences that review happened without making it capable of changing anything. Volume is a real fatigue factor, but matching the old workload is not what makes the control sound.

question: An organisation must decommission a model that has been making decisions for three years. Which consideration is most often overlooked?
options: A. Archiving the model artifacts so the version can be reinstated if needed.
B. Retaining what is needed to explain decisions the model already made.
C. Notifying the vendor that the licence will not be renewed.
D. Removing the model from the inventory to keep the register current.
rationale: Turning a model off does not end the obligations attached to what it decided. Subjects may still contest an outcome, and regulators may still ask how one was reached, so the ability to explain past decisions has to outlive the system — and it is the piece most often deleted alongside the deployment. Artifact archiving, vendor notice and inventory hygiene are all standard decommissioning steps that teams generally remember.

question: A vendor's AI feature is enabled by default in a product an organisation already uses for internal document storage. Which action is most appropriate on discovering this?
options: A. Disable the feature immediately as an unapproved change to the environment.
B. Establish what the feature does with the organisation's content, then decide.
C. Accept the change, since it arrived through an already-approved product.
D. Escalate to the board as a material third-party governance failure.
rationale: The governance question is what the feature does with content the organisation is responsible for — whether it processes documents in place, sends them anywhere, or retains them — and that determines everything else. Disabling on reflex may remove a benign capability and does not tell you whether anything already happened; accepting it because the product was approved is how unreviewed capability enters an estate; and board escalation is disproportionate before the facts are known.

question: A team is asked to make a complex model's decisions explainable to affected individuals. Which approach best serves that audience?
options: A. Publish global feature importances for the model as a whole.
B. The reasons that mattered for that individual's outcome, in plain language.
C. Release the model architecture and hyperparameters for public scrutiny.
D. Provide a confidence score alongside each decision.
rationale: An affected individual is asking why this happened to me, which is a local question — the factors that drove their outcome, in language they can act on. Global importances describe the model's average behaviour and may not explain any particular case; architecture serves researchers; and a confidence score reports certainty without giving a single reason.

question: Which practice most reduces the risk that a model reproduces historical discrimination present in its training data?
options: A. Increasing the volume of historical data used for training.
B. Examining whether the historical outcomes themselves reflect past unequal treatment.
C. Selecting a model architecture that is less prone to overfitting the training set.
D. Holding out a more recent time period for evaluation.
rationale: A model trained to predict past outcomes will reproduce whatever produced them, and if past decisions were unequal, high fidelity to that history is the failure rather than the goal. The only step that reaches the cause is interrogating what the labels record. More data adds more of the same pattern, architecture choice addresses variance, and a recent holdout detects drift rather than inherited unfairness.

question: A model is trained on data collected for a different, unrelated purpose. Which question should be resolved first?
options: A. Whether the data volume is sufficient for the new modelling task to converge at all.
B. Whether the new use is compatible with the purpose the data was collected for.
C. Whether the data can be transformed into the schema the pipeline expects.
D. Whether the original collection was technically accurate.
rationale: Purpose limitation makes compatibility a gating question, not a downstream one: if the new use is incompatible with what people were told at collection, no amount of engineering makes it usable. Volume, schema and accuracy all matter and all become relevant only once the use is permitted at all.

question: Which TWO practices most support reproducibility of a model that may need to be defended years later?
options: A. Versioning the training data alongside the code and model artifacts.
B. Recording the environment and random seeds used for the training run.
C. Storing the final model weights in a redundant location.
D. Documenting the business case that justified building the model.
E. Keeping the evaluation dashboard available to reviewers.
rationale: Reproducibility means being able to produce the same model again, and the two things most often missing are the exact data it saw and the exact conditions it ran under — code alone is not enough when the dataset has moved on and the run was stochastic. Redundant weight storage preserves the output rather than the ability to recreate it, and the business case and dashboard are governance context rather than reproduction inputs.

question: A stakeholder asks why an AI governance programme needs anything beyond the organisation's existing risk management. What is the strongest answer?
options: A. AI risk is larger in magnitude than the risks the existing programme already handles.
B. AI systems change behaviour after deployment and produce harms no control watches for.
C. AI regulation requires a separate programme with separate reporting lines.
D. Existing risk management lacks the technical expertise to assess models.
rationale: Conventional risk management assumes a system does what it was specified to do until something breaks. AI systems drift as their inputs change, and can produce harms — unfairness, degradation, misplaced confidence — that no existing control was written to detect. That is a gap in what is monitored, not a gap in seriousness. Magnitude is arguable, no regime mandates a separate programme, and expertise can be added to a function that is still looking for the wrong signals.

question: An organisation classifies an AI system as minimal risk and applies no specific controls. Two years later the system is used for a materially different purpose. What does this most illustrate?
options: A. Risk classification must be revisited when intended purpose changes.
B. Minimal-risk classifications should be avoided in favour of higher categories.
C. Classification should be performed by an external assessor.
D. Risk classification is unreliable as a governance mechanism.
rationale: Classification is a judgement about a system in a use, and it expires when the use changes. The failure is treating it as a permanent property assigned once at build time. Inflating every classification wastes assurance capacity on systems that do not need it, external assessment does not make a stale classification current, and the mechanism works — it just has to be re-run on change.

question: Three teams propose different responses to a model that has begun producing biased outputs for one customer segment. Which should be assessed FIRST?
options: A. Whether affected customers should be notified and remediated.
B. Whether the bias is ongoing and can be stopped now.
C. Whether the model should be retrained with corrected data.
D. Whether the vendor contract permits recovery of remediation costs.
rationale: Stopping accrual comes before repairing what has accrued: while the model keeps deciding, the affected population keeps growing and the remediation scope keeps moving. Notification and redress are obligations that follow, retraining is the durable fix that takes time, and contractual recovery is a commercial question that no customer's experience depends on.

question: An organisation wants one measure indicating whether its AI governance programme is working. Which is most informative?
options: A. The number of AI systems recorded in the inventory.
B. The share of deployed systems that passed the required review before release.
C. The number of staff across the organisation who completed AI governance training.
D. The number of governance policies published in the last year.
rationale: Coverage of the control at the moment it matters is the closest single proxy for whether governance is actually in the path of decisions, and it exposes the characteristic failure — systems shipping around the process. Inventory size measures how much exists, training completion measures attendance, and policy count measures writing. All three can rise while every system still ships unreviewed.

question: Referral rates are double the book average in three postcodes, which were not features. What should Kestrel establish FIRST?
options: A. Whether the model is reconstructing location from other features, and with what effect.
B. Whether the fraud team agrees the referral model remains commercially valuable.
C. Whether complaint volumes in those postcodes exceed the ombudsman's threshold.
D. Whether removing the affected postcodes from scoring is technically feasible.
rationale: A feature being absent from the input does not mean the information is absent from the model. Something in the remaining features is carrying location, and the question that governs every later decision is what that is and whether the resulting difference is justified. Commercial value, complaint thresholds and remediation feasibility all become relevant once the mechanism is understood; none of them can be judged before it.

question: Kestrel has not refreshed validation in two years, arguing that monitoring has stayed inside tolerance. What is the strongest objection?
options: A. Two years exceeds the maximum interval permitted for model validation.
B. Monitoring watches the measures chosen at launch; validation asks whether they are still the right ones.
C. Monitoring cannot detect changes in the underlying claims population.
D. Validation is required whenever a model has been in production for a full year.
rationale: The three monitored measures were selected when the model was built, and all three stayed green while a geographic disparity developed underneath them. That is exactly the blind spot revalidation exists to find: monitoring answers whether the model still does what you measured, and validation asks whether you are measuring the right things. No general rule fixes an interval at one or two years, and monitoring can detect population change — it simply was not looking for this.
